en.apparato_digerente_anatomia_orale:
FUNCTIONAL ANATOMY AND OROPHARYNGEAL PHYSIOLOGY

In summary: A continuous and specialized tubular system, approximately 9-10 meters long, that chemically and mechanically transforms food into assimilable molecules. Each section has a specific function, from mechanical grinding to the hormonal regulation of flow.

TOPOGRAPHY AND ORGANIZATION OF THE DIGESTIVE TRACT

The digestive system is configured as a continuous tube of about 9-10 meters, articulated into distinct segments by morphology and function. The journey begins with the mouth, delimited by the lips, and proceeds through the isthmus of the fauces toward the pharynx, a critical anatomical crossroads between the digestive and respiratory tracts.

From the pharynx, the bolus descends into the esophagus, a muscular conduit connecting the pharynx to the stomach. The latter, the most dilated portion (often compared to a bagpipe for its variable shape), acts as a reservoir and initial chemical reactor. Its exit is controlled by the pyloric sphincter, a ring of circular muscle fibers that regulates the passage of chyme into the intestine.

The intestine is divided into two functional sections:

Digestive & Absorptive Tract
Small Intestine (~6.8 m)

Primary site of chemical digestion and absorption. The absorption surface is amplified by circular folds, villi, and microvilli (brush border).

  • Duodenum: Receives bile and pancreatic juice; secretes Secretin and CCK for the neutralization of chyme.
  • Jejunum: Primary site for the absorption of amino acids, monosaccharides, and lipids.
  • Ileum: Site of Peyer's patches (GALT); reabsorbs bile salts and Vitamin B12. Ends with the ileocecal valve.
Reabsorptive & Fermentative Tract
Large Intestine (~1.8 m)

Devoid of villi, structured into taeniae coli and haustra. Specialized in hydro-electrolytic balance and metabolic symbiosis with the microbiota.

  • Cecum & Appendix: Entry point and immune/microbial reservoir.
  • Colon (Asc., Trans., Desc., Sigmoid): Reabsorbs water and electrolytes; the microbiota synthesizes SCFAs (butyrate, acetate, propionate) and vitamins.
  • Rectum & Anal Canal: Compaction and elimination of feces via the internal (involuntary) and external (voluntary) anal sphincters.

The inner surface, lined with mucosa, features crucial morphological specializations in the small intestine for absorption: connivent valves (circular folds of the mucosa) and intestinal villi, which exponentially multiply the exchange surface.

THE ROLE OF THE MICROBIOTA AND FECAL FORMATION

In the large intestine, digestive enzymatic activity is negligible, but the action of the microbial flora (intestinal microbiota) reigns supreme. These microorganisms perform essential functions:

  • Synthesis of vitamins (e.g., Vitamin K, B-complex).
  • Degradation of undigested food residues (fermentation and putrefaction).

The feces, expelled through the anus, are not merely food residues, but a biological complex composed largely of intestinal bacteria, desquamated epithelial cells, and water.

MASTICATION AND SWALLOWING: FROM MECHANICS TO REFLEX

Mastication is the first act of digestion, a process of mechanical grinding performed by the teeth, coordinated by the movements of the tongue and cheeks. This act is governed by nerve centers in the temporal cortex and the medulla oblongata, which activate the masticatory muscles (masseter, temporalis, pterygoids) for food breakdown.

Concurrently with mechanics, chemical digestion begins through enzymes. Enzymes are specific biological catalysts: they accelerate chemical reactions (such as hydrolysis) without being consumed, acting on specific substrates (e.g., pepsin for proteins, amylase for carbohydrates). As early as the 18th century, Lazzaro Spallanzani intuited the crucial role of gastric juices in these processes.

SALIVARY PHYSIOLOGY AND NEUROHUMORAL CONTROL

The salivary glands (parotid, sublingual, submandibular) secrete saliva, a fluid composed of 98.7% water and a complex organic and inorganic fraction:

Salivary Fraction Components and Physiological Functions
Inorganic components: Chlorides activate amylase; bicarbonates and phosphates constitute a buffer system that maintains pH near neutrality.
Organic components: Mucin (lubricant) and ptyalin (salivary amylase), which hydrolyzes starch into dextrins and maltose at neutral pH. The action of ptyalin ceases in the stomach due to inactivation by hydrochloric acid.

Salivary secretion is regulated by a nervous reflex (parasympathetic > sympathetic), triggered by mechanical, chemical, visual, or olfactory stimuli. Saliva not only promotes digestion and the formation of the food bolus, but also performs protective (teeth), gustatory, and water-regulating functions (sense of thirst).

MECHANISMS OF SWALLOWING AND PERISTALSIS

Once formed, the food bolus is swallowed. From this moment on, the process becomes involuntary, controlled by the swallowing center in the medulla.

Swallowing is a complex reflex act that ensures airway safety:

Phase 1
Elevation of the soft palate to close the choanae.
↓
Phase 2
Lowering of the epiglottis (via the hyoid bone) to protect the larynx.
↓
Respiratory Protection
Swallowing apnea: temporary cessation of breathing.

In the esophagus, the bolus is pushed by peristalsis: waves of muscular contraction and relaxation that propagate along the entire digestive tract. The peristaltic wave slows down at the cardiac sphincter, allowing its relaxation and the entry of the bolus into the stomach.
en.apparato_digerente_fisiologia_gastro_met:
GASTRODUODENAL PHYSIOLOGY, ABSORPTION, AND HEPATIC METABOLISM

In summary: The transition from the stomach to the intestine represents a highly precise system of hormonal and neural regulation. From acid secretion controlled by proton pumps to duodenal zymogen cascades, the body breaks down macromolecules into assimilable monomers. Membrane transporters on the brush border then guide specific absorption, conveying water-soluble nutrients to the liver via the portal vein and complex lipids into the lymphatic system.

1. GASTROPHYSIOLOGY AND ACID SECRETION

Gastric digestion converts the food bolus into chyme through intense motor activity (antral peristaltic waves) and chemical-enzymatic action. Acid secretion by parietal cells is integrated into three distinct physiological phases:

  • Cephalic Phase (~30%): Triggered by visual, olfactory, gustatory, or cognitive stimuli. Activates the vagus nerve (CN X), which releases acetylcholine and directly stimulates parietal cells and gastrin G cells.
  • Gastric Phase (~60%): Provoked by mechanical distension of the stomach and the presence of luminal peptides/amino acids. Represents the phase of peak secretion.
  • Intestinal Phase (~10%): Triggered by the initial entry of chyme into the duodenum; initially stimulatory, it rapidly becomes inhibitory through the release of enterogastrones (secretin, somatostatin).

MOLECULAR MECHANISM OF THE PARIETAL CELL

The secretion of hydrochloric acid (HCl) by parietal (oxyntic) cells relies on the transmembrane enzyme H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump). This pump extrudes H+ ions into the gastric lumen in exchange for K+ ions against a concentration gradient, with direct ATP consumption.

Mediator Parietal Receptor Transduction Pathway Physiological Effect
Histamine (from ECL cells) H2 Gs protein → Adenylate Cyclase → ↑ cAMP → PKA Strong activation of the H+/K+ Pump
Acetylcholine (Vagal) M3 Gq protein → PLC → IP3/DAG → ↑ cytosolic Ca2+ Activation of gastric acid secretion
Gastrin (from G Cells) CCKB (CCK2) Gq protein → PLC → ↑ cytosolic Ca2+ Parietal stimulation and Histamine release from ECL
Somatostatin / PGE2 SST2 / EP3 Gi protein → Adenylate Cyclase Inhibition → ↓ cAMP Potent inhibition of acid secretion

The gastric environment reaches pH levels between 1.5 and 2.0. The mucosa protects itself from autodigestive damage via the gastric mucosal barrier, composed of a viscous layer of hydrated mucin secreted by foveolar cells and a superficial alkaline gradient maintained by active bicarbonate secretion (HCO3-).

Pepsinogen (an inactive proenzyme secreted by chief cells) undergoes autocatalytic cleavage at pH < 5.0, transforming into pepsin, an endopeptidase with an optimal catalytic activity at pH 1.8–2.0 that cleaves internal peptide bonds in proteins. Parietal cells also secrete Intrinsic Factor, a glycoprotein essential for Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

2. PANCREATIC AND BILIARY SECRETIONS IN THE DUODENUM

In the duodenum, acidic chyme is neutralized and subjected to hydrolysis by the secretory arsenal of the exocrine pancreas and biliary tract.

  • Secretin: Released by duodenal S cells in response to luminal pH drop (< 4.5). Stimulates ductal cells to secrete a fluid rich in HCO3-, raising duodenal pH to optimal values for enzymatic catalysis (pH 7.5–8.0).
  • Cholecystokinin (CCK): Released by I cells in response to fatty acids and amino acids. Stimulates pancreatic acinar cells to release zymogens and induces gallbladder contraction along with relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi.

PANCREATIC ZYMOGEN ACTIVATION

To prevent autodigestion of pancreatic tissue, proteolytic enzymes are synthesized and secreted as inactive proenzymes. The activation cascade occurs exclusively within the duodenal lumen:

Step 1 · Brush Border
Enterokinase Priming
The membrane-bound enzyme enterokinase cleaves a hexapeptide from trypsinogen, converting it into active Trypsin.
↓
Step 2 · Autocatalysis & Amplification
Pancreatic Enzymatic Cascade
Trypsin activates further trypsinogen and cleaves other zymogens: chymotrypsinogen → chymotrypsin; proelastase → elastase; procarboxypeptidase → carboxypeptidase A and B.
↓
Step 3 · Carbohydrate Hydrolysis
Action of Pancreatic Amylase
Pancreatic Amylase (secreted in active form) hydrolyzes α-(1,4) starch bonds, yielding maltose, maltotriose, and limit dextrins.

BILIARY PHYSIOLOGY AND LIPID EMULSIFICATION

Bile produced by hepatocytes and concentrated in the gallbladder lacks digestive enzymes, but contains bile salts (derived from cholesterol via hydroxylation and conjugation with glycine or taurine, such as glycocholic and taurocholic acid).

As amphipathic molecules, bile salts reduce the surface tension of lipid droplets, breaking them down into a fine emulsion. This dramatically increases the surface area exposed to pancreatic lipase (acting synergistically with colipase). Hydrolysis products and bile salts assemble into mixed micelles (3-10 nm diameter), essential for lipid diffusion to the enterocyte absorptive surface.

3. MOLECULAR MECHANISMS OF INTESTINAL ABSORPTION

Absorption occurs predominantly in the jejunum and ileum thanks to villi and microvilli on the brush border that amplify the epithelial surface area.

Nutrient Apical (Luminal) Transporter Molecular Mechanism Basolateral Efflux
Glucose / Galactose SGLT1 Na+-dependent secondary active cotransport (driven by Na+/K+-ATPase gradient) GLUT2 (Facilitated diffusion)
Fructose GLUT5 Facilitated diffusion independent of sodium and energy GLUT2 (Facilitated diffusion)
Dipeptides / Tripeptides PepT1 H+-dependent secondary active cotransport (coupled to NHE3 exchanger) Cytosolic hydrolysis to free AAs → AA Transporters
Free Amino Acids Systems B0, ASC, XA- Secondary active transporters specific for neutral, basic, or acidic amino acids Facilitated diffusion via basolateral transporters

LIPID ABSORPTION AND CHYLOMICRON FORMATION

Monoglycerides and long-chain fatty acids (> 12 carbon atoms) released from micelles cross the apical membrane via diffusion and specific transporters (e.g., FAT/CD36).

Inside the enterocyte's smooth endoplasmic reticulum, these products are re-esterified into triglycerides. Together with esterified cholesterol and apolipoproteins (specifically ApoB-48), they are assembled in the Golgi apparatus into chylomicrons. Due to their large size, chylomicrons are secreted into lacteals (lymphatic vessels) and enter systemic circulation via the thoracic duct, bypassing the liver initially.

Water absorption (7-8 liters/day) occurs passively via osmosis following active sodium reabsorption. In the colon, the epithelium expresses aldosterone-regulated ENaC sodium channels, allowing compaction of chyme and near-total recovery of residual electrolytes.

4. HEPATIC FIRST-PASS METABOLISM

Water-soluble nutrients (monosaccharides, amino acids, short-chain fatty acids, and electrolytes) absorbed by the intestinal epithelium are collected by mesenteric veins and drained into the Portal Vein, reaching the liver directly.

The liver serves as the central metabolic coordinator before nutrients are distributed to systemic circulation:

  • Fate of Carbohydrates: In the postprandial state, insulin promotes hepatic extraction of glucose via GLUT2 and its storage through glycogen synthesis. Excess glucose is directed toward de novo lipogenesis.
  • Fate of Amino Acids: Utilized for the synthesis of plasma proteins (albumin, clotting factors) and tissue proteins, or routed to deamination. Toxic amino groups released as ammonia are cleared via the Urea Cycle in hepatocytes.
  • Fate of Lipids: Portal short-chain fatty acids and chylomicron remnants cleared from circulation are processed by hepatocytes. The liver synthesizes and secretes Very Low-Density Lipoproteins (VLDL) to distribute endogenous triglycerides to peripheral tissues.
en.apparato_digerente_patofisiologia_clinic:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND CLINICAL ASPECTS

In brief: Digestive health is not merely the absence of disease, but a dynamic balance between protective factors (mucosa, enzymes, flora) and aggressive factors (acids, toxins, pathogens). Understanding pathological mechanisms is essential for precise diagnosis and targeted therapy.

GASTRODUODENAL ULCER: THE IMBALANCE

An ulcer is a lesion penetrating beyond the mucosa into the submucosa and often the muscularis. It results from the disruption of epithelial physiological balance:

Aggressive Factors
Chemical & Bacterial Insults
Hydrochloric acid (HCl), pepsin, Helicobacter pylori infection (urease activity/toxins), and NSAIDs.
Protective Factors
Mucosal Barrier Defenses
Mucin layer, Bicarbonate secretion (HCO₃⁻), adequate blood microcirculation, and Prostaglandins E₂.
▼
Clinical Picture
Epithelial Damage & Symptomatic Presentation
Postprandial epigastric pain (early in gastric ulcers, late/relieved by food in duodenal ulcers), nausea, and risk of complications (hemorrhage, perforation).

Helicobacter pylori is a microaerophilic Gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the gastric mucosa. By producing urease, it converts urea into ammonia and CO₂, neutralizing local acid to survive and releasing cytotoxins (VacA, CagA) that damage epithelial cells.

MALABSORPTION: WHEN ABSORPTION FAILS

Malabsorption defines the reduced ability of the small intestine to assimilate nutrients, electrolytes, or vitamins. The primary etiopathogeneses include:

  • Enzyme and digestive deficiencies: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, lactase deficiency.
  • Structural mucosal damage: Villous atrophy in celiac disease, transmural inflammation in Crohn's disease, radiation therapy effects.
  • Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO): Abnormal proliferation in the small intestine competing for nutrients (e.g., vitamin B12).
  • Reduced absorptive surface: Short bowel syndrome from surgical resection.

Key symptoms include steatorrhea (evacuation of undigested fats), weight loss, iron-deficiency or megaloblastic anemia, osteopenia from Vitamin D/Calcium deficiency, and abdominal bloating.

IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME (IBS)

IBS is a functional gastrointestinal disorder with a multifactorial etiology, lacking structural lesions detectable by conventional imaging. Pathogenesis includes:

  • Visceral hypersensitivity: Lowered pain threshold to mechanical and distension stimuli.
  • Intestinal dysmotility: Altered peristaltic waves (hyper/hypomotility).
  • Quantitative and qualitative dysbiosis: Alteration of the indigenous microbiome.
  • Gut-Brain Axis dysregulation: Psychosocial modulation and altered responses to stress.

Diagnosis is based on the Rome IV Criteria and is a diagnosis of exclusion of organic diseases (IBD, celiac disease, neoplasms).

DIGESTIVE NEOPLASMS: COLON AND STOMACH CANCER

Malignant tumors of the digestive tract represent a primary share of oncological pathology. Most colorectal carcinomas originate from adenomatous polyps through the adenoma-carcinoma sequence (accumulation of mutations in APC, KRAS, p53).

Risk factors include advanced age, diets high in red/processed meats and low fiber, obesity, smoking, and hereditary syndromes (Lynch, FAP).

Symptoms (often late) include change in bowel habits, hematochezia or melena, insidious microcytic anemia, and weight loss. Screening (FOBT and colonoscopy with preventive polypectomy) drastically reduces mortality.

Gastric carcinoma is associated with chronic atrophic gastritis from H. pylori, consumption of salted/smoked foods, and nitrosamines. Diagnosis is often delayed due to non-specific early symptoms (mild dyspepsia).

DIAGNOSTICS: TOOLS AND APPROACHES

The diagnosis of digestive diseases utilizes:

Diagnostic Modality Methodology / Target Clinical Applications & Findings
Blood & Stool Tests Systemic biomarkers Evaluation of anemia (Hb, ferritin), inflammation (CRP, ESR), pancreatic enzymes (amylase/lipase), and FOBT.
Digestive Endoscopy EGD & Colonoscopy Direct mucosal inspection, histological biopsy sampling, and therapeutic procedures (polypectomy).
Diagnostic Imaging US, CT, MRI, MRCP Neoplastic staging, intestinal wall examination, and mapping of the biliary-pancreatic tree.
Functional & Breath Tests Labeled substrates (e.g., ¹³C-Urea, Lactose) Non-invasive diagnosis of H. pylori infection, carbohydrate malabsorption, and SIBO.
en.apparato_digerente_microbiota_asse_intes:
MICROBIOTA AND THE GUT-BRAIN AXIS

In brief: The intestine is not just a digestive organ, but a complex ecosystem and a neural processing center. The gut microbiota (the community of microorganisms inhabiting it) constantly communicates with the brain through neural, hormonal, and immune pathways, influencing mood, behavior, and overall health.

THE GUT MICROBIOTA: A SYMBIOTIC ORGANISM

The gut microbiota consists of trillions of bacteria, viruses, fungi, and archaea, with a genetic pool (metagenome) that exceeds the human genome by 150 times. It is not merely a "guest", but a true acquired metabolic organ.

Its main physiological functions include:

  • Digestion of indigestible substrates: Breakdown of fibers and resistant starches producing short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as butyrate, propionate, and acetate, essential for colonic mucosal health.
  • Synthesis of essential micronutrients: Biosynthesis of vitamin K, vitamin B12, folates, and biotin.
  • Barrier effect and pathogen protection: Competition for ecological niches, secretion of bacteriocins, and maintenance of tight junction integrity.
  • Immune system modulation: Regulation and development of GALT (up to 70% of the body's lymphoid tissue resides in the gut).

Dysbiosis (qualitative and quantitative alteration of the microbiota) compromises this equilibrium, linking to inflammatory (IBD, IBS), dysmetabolic (obesity, type 2 diabetes), allergic, and neuropsychiatric disorders.

THE GUT-BRAIN AXIS: A CONSTANT DIALOGUE

The gut-brain axis represents a bidirectional communication network connecting the Enteric Nervous System (ENS) to the Central Nervous System (CNS). This dialogue unfolds along four main pathways:

Pathway 1 · Neural
Vagus Nerve and ENS
Primary neural highway for rapid transmission of afferent signals from the intestinal epithelium to the brainstem and vice versa.
Pathway 2 · Endocrine
Enteroendocrine Cells
Secretion of systemic peptides and hormones (e.g., serotonin, ghrelin, leptin) regulating appetite, mood, and stress response.
Pathway 3 · Immune
Cytokines and GALT
Inflammatory mediators produced locally in the gut can cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB), influencing brain function.
Pathway 4 · Metabolic
Microbial Metabolites
SCFAs (butyrate), neurotransmitters, and tryptophan derivatives entering the bloodstream to act directly on central receptors.

NEUROTRANSMITTERS AND MICROBIOTA

The gut microbiota operates as an advanced neurochemical hub, directly producing or modulating the synthesis of key neuromediators:

Neurotransmitter Microbial Origin / Mechanism Physiological Role & Clinical Impact
Serotonin (5-HT) ~90% produced by enterochromaffin cells stimulated by bacterial metabolites. Regulation of gut motility, mood, sleep, and appetite. Alterations linked to anxiety and depression.
GABA (γ-aminobutyrate) Synthesized directly by strains such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. Primary central inhibitory neurotransmitter; exerts anxiolytic and relaxing effects.
Dopamine Synthesis and tissue modulation driven by specific microbial populations. Regulation of reward circuits, motivation, and motor coordination.
Acetylcholine Produced by several commensal bacterial strains within the enteric environment. Modulation of memory, cognitive functions, and visceral smooth muscle contraction.

Scientific evidence underscores how targeted modulation of the microbiota (via probiotics, prebiotics, or fecal microbiota transplantation FMT) represents a new therapeutic frontier in psychiatry and neurology.

IMMUNITY AND MICROBIOTA

The microbiota is essential for the development and homeostasis of the immune system. By interacting with mucosal immune cells (T lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells), it maintains a constant balance between immunological tolerance (towards food antigens and commensals) and defensive response (against pathogens).

Early dysbiosis during the first years of life can alter immune maturation, predisposing to autoimmune diseases, allergies, and asthma. SCFAs (particularly butyrate) exert potent anti-inflammatory effects and strengthen the intestinal barrier, preventing hyperpermeability ("leaky gut").

KEY FACTORS SHAPING MICROBIAL COMPOSITION

The structure and diversity of the gut microbial ecosystem are shaped by four key factors:

Nutrition
Diet and Nutrients
Diets rich in fibers and fermented foods promote bacterial biodiversity; saturated fats and refined sugars foster dysbiosis.
Pharmacology
Pharmacological Treatments
Antibiotics cause drastic alterations to the microbiome; PPIs, NSAIDs, and psychotropic drugs also impact its composition.
Lifestyle
Stress and Environment
Chronic stress, sleep deprivation, and sedentary habits alter gut motility and mucosal barrier function.
Early Development
Birth and Breastfeeding
Vaginal delivery and breastfeeding foster colonization by a more diverse and beneficial microflora.

Maintaining gut microbiota eubiosis is a fundamental pillar for overall health, from the gut to the brain.
en.apparato_digerente_approfondimento_bioch:
BIOCHEMICAL DEEP DIVE

In brief: Digestion is not limited to mechanical breakdown but is the starting point for complex metabolic pathways. Understanding enzyme kinetics, the Krebs Cycle (the cell's energy engine), and the Urea Cycle (the nitrogen disposal system) is fundamental to understanding how nutrients are converted into energy and biomolecules, and how the body manages toxic waste products.

ENZYME KINETICS: THE MICHAELIS-MENTEN EQUATION

The rate at which an enzyme catalyzes a reaction is not linear with substrate concentration but follows a hyperbolic curve described by the Michaelis-Menten equation. This model describes the relationship between reaction velocity (V) and substrate concentration ([S]).

The fundamental equation is:

V = Vmax [S] Km + [S]

Where:

  • Vmax is the theoretical maximum reaction velocity, reached when all enzyme active sites are saturated with substrate.
  • Km (Michaelis Constant) is the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is half of Vmax. It is an inverse index of the enzyme's affinity for the substrate: a low Km indicates high affinity (the enzyme works efficiently even at low substrate concentrations), while a high Km indicates low affinity.

Michaelis-Menten kinetics are fundamental for understanding metabolic regulation and pharmacodynamics. Enzyme inhibitors alter kinetic parameters in characteristic ways:

Inhibition Type Effect on Vmax Effect on Km Mechanism of Action
Competitive Unchanged Increases (apparent) Inhibitor binds to the free active site. Overcome by increasing [S].
Non-Competitive Decreases Unchanged Inhibitor binds to an allosteric site on both free enzyme and ES complex.
Uncompetitive Decreases Decreases (apparent) Inhibitor binds exclusively to the Enzyme-Substrate (ES) complex.

THE KREBS CYCLE (TRICARBOXYLIC ACID CYCLE)

The Krebs Cycle, located in the mitochondrial matrix, is the central metabolic pathway for the complete oxidation of nutrients. It is the convergence point for the catabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, and amino acids, and the primary source of reducing power (NADH, FADH2) for the respiratory chain.

Initial Phase · Step 1
Condensation & Citrate Synthesis
Acetyl-CoA (2C) condenses with Oxaloacetate (4C) to form Citrate (6C). Irreversible and strongly exergonic reaction catalyzed by citrate synthase.
↓
Oxidative Phase · Steps 2 - 4
Isomerization & Oxidative Decarboxylation
Citrate is converted to Isocitrate and undergoes two successive oxidative decarboxylations (via isocitrate DH and α-ketoglutarate DH), releasing 2 CO2 and generating 2 NADH + Succinyl-CoA (4C).
↓
Energetic Phase · Step 5
Substrate-Level Phosphorylation
Cleavage of the high-energy thioester bond of Succinyl-CoA (via succinyl-CoA synthetase) is coupled to direct synthesis of 1 GTP / ATP and formation of Succinate.
↓
Regeneration Phase · Steps 6 - 8
Dehydrogenation & Oxaloacetate Regeneration
Succinate is oxidized to Fumarate (generating 1 FADH2 via succinate DH), hydrated to L-Malate, and finally oxidized to Oxaloacetate (generating 1 NADH via malate DH), restarting the cycle.

Net yield per oxidized Acetyl-CoA molecule:

  • 3 NADH (transfer 6 high-energy electrons to the respiratory chain).
  • 1 FADH2 (electron donor to mitochondrial Complex II).
  • 1 GTP / ATP (generated via substrate-level phosphorylation by succinyl-CoA synthetase).
  • 2 CO2 (waste byproducts of oxidative decarboxylation).

The Krebs Cycle is an amphibolic pathway (both catabolic and anabolic): it provides intermediates for gluconeogenesis, fatty acid synthesis, amino acids, and porphyrins. It is allosterically regulated by energy charge (ATP/ADP) and redox state (NADH/NAD+).

THE UREA CYCLE: NITROGEN DISPOSAL

Amino acid catabolism releases amino groups (-NH2) as ammonia (NH3/NH4+), which is neurotoxic at micromolar levels. The liver converts ammonia into urea via a metabolic cycle requiring spatial coordination between the mitochondrion and cytosol.

Mitochondrial Phase · Step 1
Carbamoyl Phosphate Formation
NH4+ + HCO3- + 2 ATP → Carbamoyl Phosphate + 2 ADP + Pi. Catalyzed by Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS I), allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate.
↓
Mitochondrial Phase · Step 2
Citrulline Synthesis & Cytosolic Transport
Carbamoyl Phosphate reacts with Ornithine (via Ornithine Transcarbamylase - OTC) forming Citrulline, which is translocated to the cytosol.
↓
Cytosolic Phase · Steps 3 & 4
Condensation & Argininosuccinate Cleavage
Citrulline binds to Aspartate (donating the second amino group) consuming 1 ATP → AMP + PPi (2 high-energy bonds). Argininosuccinate is then cleaved into Arginine and Fumarate (Krebs link).
↓
Cytosolic / Final Phase · Step 5
Arginine Hydrolysis & Ornithine Regeneration
Arginase cleaves Arginine, releasing Urea (for renal excretion) and regenerating Ornithine, which re-enters the mitochondrion.

The cycle consumes the stoichiometric equivalent of 4 high-energy phosphate bonds (3 ATP → 2 ADP + 1 AMP) per molecule of urea produced. Genetic defects in urea cycle enzymes (e.g., OTC deficiency) cause severe hyperammonemia, requiring protein restriction and alternative nitrogen scavengers.

METABOLIC INTEGRATION: ENERGY FLOW

These three systems operate in tight metabolic coordination:

  • Fumarate produced in the urea cycle directly enters the mitochondrion to feed the Krebs Cycle (Krebs-urea bicycle).
  • ATP generated by the respiratory chain via Krebs/NADH drives the energetic cost of the urea cycle and hepatic biosynthesis.
  • Enzyme kinetic parameters (Km and Vmax) govern the liver's metabolic flexibility when shifting between postprandial and fasted states.

Understanding these interconnections is vital for clinical biochemistry, laying the groundwork to diagnose inherited metabolic disorders, hepatic encephalopathy, and evaluate nutritional status.

en.recover_energy: Recover the energy used by organs.
en.food_transformation: The body cannot use food immediately. It must be transformed. This process is called
en.glands_release: During this process, special organs (glands) release chemicals. These substances help break food down into smaller pieces.
en.digestion_process: Digestion is therefore a process that
en.until_absorbable: until it becomes absorbable by the body.
en.digestive_tube: The digestive system is like a long tube from the mouth to the anus. It consists of several sections, each with a different shape, length, and function.
en.mouth_desc: : the entry point for food. Closed by the lips in front and connected to the pharynx behind.
en.pharynx_desc: : meeting point between food and air. Food passes into the esophagus, air into the lungs.
en.esophagus_desc: : tube connecting the pharynx to the stomach.
en.stomach_desc: : the widest part of the tube. Shaped like a bagpipe. Shape varies by person.
en.intestine_desc: : follows the stomach. Divided into two parts: small and large.
en.small_intestine_desc: It is about 6 meters and 80 centimeters long. It has three parts:
en.duodenum_desc: : digestive juices from the liver and pancreas arrive here. They help digest food.
en.ileum_desc: : last part of the small intestine. Connects to the large intestine.
en.large_intestine_desc: It is about 1 meter and 80 centimeters long. It has these parts:
en.cecum_text: beginning of the large intestine. The ileum connects here via a valve: the ileocecal valve.
en.ascending_colon_text: rises on the right side of the abdomen.
en.transverse_colon_text: runs from right to left, below the liver.
en.anal_sphincter_text: muscle that opens and closes the anus. Allows fecal expulsion.
en.intestinal_surface: The inner surface of the intestine
en.intestinal_surface_intro: Inside, the intestine has a special mucosa. In the small intestine there are:
en.valves_text: folds of the mucosa. Increase surface area.
en.villi_text: small projections. Absorb nutrients from food.
en.villi_description: They are like tiny hairs that capture digested sugars, proteins, and fats.
en.colon_function_intro: The large intestine digests little. But it plays an important role thanks to the bacteria living inside it (gut flora).
en.vitamin_production: Help produce certain vitamins (such as vitamin K).
en.fiber_digestion: Digest some food components that the rest of the intestine cannot process.
en.colon_function_note: Although beneficial, too many bacteria or the wrong types can cause diseases. For this reason, from a medical standpoint, the large intestine is studied more for diseases than for its normal function.
en.feces_composition: Feces are not just food remnants. They consist of:
en.digestive_waste: Material from the digestive tract (such as dead cells and mucus).
en.feces_expulsion: Feces are expelled outside through the anus, controlled by the anal sphincter muscle.
en.chewing_swallowing_process: Food is broken down by the teeth and sent to the stomach through the esophagus.
en.stomach_mixing: Then food reaches the stomach, where it is mixed with gastric juices to form a semi-liquid mass.
en.chewing_intro: Chewing is the first step of digestion.
en.chewing_process: Teeth cut, break, and crush food. The tongue and cheeks move food around the mouth, mixing it with saliva.
en.bolus_formation_processo: This process forms a soft ball called a food bolus. The bolus is easier to swallow.
en.jaw_control: Jaw movements are controlled by the brain, particularly by areas in the medulla and motor cortex. The muscles involved are:
en.digestive_enzymes: Enzymes: the small helpers of digestion
en.enzymes_function: Enzymes are substances that help transform food. They are like catalysts: they speed up chemical reactions without changing themselves.
en.enzymes_examples_intro: Each enzyme works on only one type of food. Examples:
en.pepsin_function_not_fats: Pepsin digests proteins, not fats or sugars.
en.rennet_function: Rennet causes milk casein to solidify.
en.maltase_function: Maltase breaks down maltose, but not sucrose.
en.enzymes_stability: Enzymes can be damaged by heat or toxic substances. But if used properly, they last a long time.
en.spallanzani_discovery: As early as the 1700s, scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani realized that stomach juices (containing enzymes) transform food.
en.glands_list_intro: Three pairs of glands produce saliva:
en.saliva_composition_details: Saliva is mostly water (98.7%). It also contains organic and inorganic substances.
en.chlorides_function: Chlorides: help the amylase enzyme work.
en.bicarbonates_phosphates_function: Bicarbonates and phosphates: maintain saliva pH close to neutral. This is important because enzymes work best in this environment.
en.mucin_function: Mucin: makes saliva viscous. Helps lubricate food and the inside of the mouth.
en.enzymes_saliva: Enzymes: the most important is ptyalin.
en.ptyalin_action: Ptyalin attacks the starch present in food.
en.ptyalin_breakdown: It breaks it down into small parts called dextrins and maltose.
en.cooked_starch: The starch is cooked (e.g., pasta, potatoes).
en.neutral_ph: The pH is neutral (as in the mouth).
en.ptyalin_stomach_inactivation: In the stomach, hydrochloric acid stops the action of ptyalin. So its work ends there.
en.bolus_formation: Promotes the formation of the food bolus.
en.mucin_lubrication: Mucin lubricates food and protects the esophagus.
en.water_balance: Regulates water turnover in the body: thirst is an important signal.
en.saliva_production_continuous: Saliva is always produced, but in varying amounts.
en.food_in_mouth: There is food in the mouth.
en.dry_strong_taste: Food is dry or has a strong flavor.
en.sight_smell_thought_food_remember: You see, smell, or think about food (or just remember it).
en.saliva_reflex_control: The process is controlled by a nervous reflex.
en.oral_stimuli: Stimuli in the mouth (touch, taste) activate receptors.
en.signal_to_bulb: The signal goes to the medulla in the brain.
en.brain_to_glands: The medulla sends an order to the salivary glands.
en.parasympathetic_nerves: Fibers of the parasympathetic nervous system stimulate saliva production. They have a stronger effect than sympathetic nervous system fibers.
en.glands_acini_structure: Salivary glands have the shape of small clusters (like grape acini). But they produce different types of saliva:
en.parotid_saliva: Parotid: produces clear, liquid saliva. Rich in ptyalin. Exits near the upper second molar through the Stensen's duct.
en.sublingual_saliva: Sublingual: produces thick, viscous saliva. Rich in mucin, but without ptyalin. Has many small ducts (15–30), each with its own opening under the tongue.
en.submandibular_saliva: Submandibular: produces mixed saliva. Contains both ptyalin and mucin. Opens on the sides of the lingual frenulum via Wharton's duct.
en.mouth_moisture_benefits: Thanks to these glands, the mouth stays moist, food is properly prepared for the stomach, and digestion can begin correctly.
en.chewed_food_bolus: After chewing, food becomes a soft, uniform mixture. It is called a food bolus.
en.bolus_to_pharynx: The bolus passes from the mouth to the pharynx. This passage is called swallowing.
en.swallowing_automatic: From this moment on, food is no longer under our control. Its movement is automatic. It is managed by reflexes controlled by the medulla.
en.soft_palate_lift: The soft palate rises. It blocks the passage to the nose.
en.epiglottis_blocks: The epiglottis lowers. It covers the larynx. Prevents food from entering the airways.
en.swallowing_apnea: Breathing stops for a moment: this is swallowing apnea.
en.peristalsis_description: The esophagus pushes the bolus toward the stomach through muscular movements.
en.peristalsis_definition: These movements are called peristalsis. They are slow waves of contraction and relaxation:
en.contraction_wave: A segment of the esophagus contracts and pushes the bolus forward.
en.relaxation_wave: The next segment relaxes to receive it.
en.wave_continuation: Then it contracts in turn, and so on.
en.peristalsis_continuation: Peristalsis begins in the esophagus and continues throughout the digestive tract.
en.cardias_function: The bolus reaches the end of the esophagus. Here it meets a muscle called the cardia. It is a sphincter: it opens and closes.
en.cardias_opening: The peristaltic wave slows down. The cardiac sphincter relaxes and opens. The bolus enters the stomach.
en.gastric_mixing: In the stomach, food is mixed with gastric juices to become a creamy substance.
en.next_step_small_intestine: Subsequently, the partially digested food enters the small intestine, where nutrient separation occurs.
en.gastric_digestion_duration: How long does digestion last in the stomach?
en.digestion_time_factors: It depends on the type and amount of food.
en.average_digestion_time: For a normal meal, it takes about 3–4 hours.
en.gastric_transformations: During this time, food undergoes two types of transformation:
en.mechanical_digestion: Mechanical: stomach movements that mix the food.
en.stomach_peristalsis: The stomach muscles contract in waves: this is peristalsis. These movements:
en.hunger_sensation: Even when the stomach is empty, it can contract strongly. This causes the sensation of hunger.
en.stomach_wall_layers: The stomach walls have multiple layers. The main ones are:
en.muscular_tunic: Muscular tunic: made of three layers of fibers:
en.mucosa_tunic: Mucosal tunic: lines the inside of the stomach.
en.gastric_pits_glands: The mucosa has many grooves. It forms hexagonal areas: these are the gastric areas. At the center of each area there are openings: this is where the gastric glands empty.
en.glands_microstructure: They are millions of tiny tubes. They produce gastric juice.
en.chief_cells: Chief cells: produce an inactive substance called pepsinogen.
en.parietal_cells: Parietal cells (or oxyntic): produce hydrochloric acid.
en.gastric_juice_composition: It is a clear liquid composed of:
en.pepsin_function: It is the enzyme that digests proteins.
en.pepsinogen_activation: It is not immediately present as an active enzyme. It is first produced as pepsinogen (inactive form).
en.hcl_activates_pepsin: In the stomach, hydrochloric acid transforms pepsinogen into pepsin.
en.proteins_to_peptones: Digests proteins, breaking them into smaller pieces: peptones.
en.pepsin_autocatalysis: Helps transform more pepsinogen into pepsin.
en.acidic_environment: Creates an acidic environment: necessary for pepsin to work.
en.bacteria_killing: Kills many bacteria present in food (antiseptic action).
en.intrinsic_factor_production: Enables the production of intrinsic factor, essential for vitamin B12 absorption.
en.spallanzani_acid_observation: Lazzaro Spallanzani already observed that meat immersed in gastric juice decomposes more slowly. This demonstrates its antiputrefactive power.
en.rennin_in_infants: It is an enzyme present in the gastric juice of infants.
en.milk_coagulation: It solidifies milk, turning it into a denser mass.
en.milk_retention: Milk stays in the stomach longer.
en.prolonged_digestion: Pepsin has more time to digest milk proteins.
en.gastric_lipase: Gastric lipase: begins to digest fats. But its role is small, especially in adults.
en.mucin_protection: Mucin: protects the stomach wall. Forms a barrier against hydrochloric acid and pepsin. Without it, the stomach would digest itself.
en.gastric_juice_triggers: It is not produced continuously. It starts when:
en.sight_smell_thought_food: You see, smell, or think about food.
en.cephalic_phase: Cephalic phase: Begins even before eating. Controlled by the vagus nerves. Triggered by sight, smell, and thought of food.
en.gastric_phase: Gastric phase: Starts when food enters the stomach. The pyloric mucosa releases a hormone: gastrin. Gastrin stimulates increased production of gastric juice.
en.chyme_formation: At the end of gastric digestion, food changes appearance. It becomes a liquid, whitish substance called chyme.
en.chyme_release: Chyme leaves the stomach in small spurts. This happens thanks to strong contractions of the pyloric antrum (the final part of the stomach).
en.pyloric_sphincter_control: The pyloric sphincter opens in a controlled way:
en.sphincter_opens_periodically: It opens periodically to allow chyme to pass into the duodenum.
en.duodenal_reflex: As soon as some chyme enters the duodenum, a reflex is triggered that closes the sphincter. Thus, the rest of the chyme waits.
en.meccanismo_svuotamento_lento: This mechanism allows for a slow and regulated emptying, giving the rest of the intestine time to digest properly.
en.titolo_intestino_tenue_crasso: DIGESTION IN THE SMALL INTESTINE, THE FUNCTION OF THE LARGE INTESTINE
en.desc_fase_3_p1: In the small intestine, nutrients are separated and prepared for absorption.
en.desc_fase_3_p2: Finally, nutrients pass from the intestine into the blood and are distributed throughout the body to produce energy and make the cells work.
en.titolo_cont_tenue: Digestion Continues in the Small Intestine
en.parz_digerito: Food is only partially digested in the stomach. The most important part of digestion takes place in the small intestine.
en.enzimi_fonti: Enzymes arrive here from three sources:
en.duodeno_liquidi: All these fluids are released into the duodenum, the first section of the small intestine.
en.microvilli_aumento: The inside of the small intestine isn't smooth. It has folds, villi, and microvilli that vastly increase the surface area.
en.villi_desc: The intestinal villi are small hair-like projections. They are mainly found in the ileum (the last section of the small intestine). There can be up to 1000 per cm².
en.villi_no_crasso: Villi are not present in the large intestine.
en.villo_strato_esterno: An outer layer of epithelial cells.
en.villo_cellule_contrazione: Contractile cells to move the villus
en.succo_enterico_produzione: It is produced by the glands of the small intestine: the glands of Lieberkühn (and the glands of Brunner in the duodenum as well).
en.succo_enterico_alcalino: Alkaline: it neutralizes the acidity of the chyme.
en.succo_enterico_muco: Rich in mucus: it protects the mucosa.
en.succo_enterico_enzimi: Strong in enzymes: they complete digestion.
en.enterochinasi_azione: Enterokinase: activates trypsinogen (from the pancreas) → becomes trypsin.
en.nucleasi_azione: Nucleases: digest nucleic acids (DNA and RNA).
en.titolo_ormoni_duodeno: Duodenal Hormones: The Digestion Control Center
en.ormoni_produzione_desc: The duodenum mucosa produces hormones that control digestion.
en.secretina_rilascio: It is released when the chyme is acidic.
en.secretina_stimolo_bicarbonati: It stimulates the pancreas to produce fluid rich in bicarbonates (to neutralize the acid).
en.secretina_stop_gastrico: It stops the production of gastric juice in the stomach: it's no longer needed!
en.cck_stimolo_enzimi: It stimulates the pancreas to release digestive enzymes.
en.cck_contrazione_colecisti: It contracts the gallbladder: so bile enters the duodenum.
en.cck_aumento_movimenti: It increases the movements of the small intestine.
en.pancreatico_arrivo: It reaches the duodenum through two ducts:
en.pancreatico_contenuto: It is produced by the pancreas and contains three main enzymes:
en.tripsina_azione: Transforms proteins and peptones into amino acids.
en.tripsina_altri_enzimi: It, in turn, activates other pancreatic enzymes.
en.amilasi_azione_amido: Digests starch that hasn't been transformed yet.
en.amilasi_azione_disaccaridi: It breaks it down into disaccharides (e.g., maltose).
en.lipasi_azione_acidi: It breaks them down into fatty acids and glycerol.
en.lipasi_bisogno_bile: But lipase cannot act on fats right away. First, the bile from the liver is needed.
en.titolo_bile_lipasi: How do Bile and Lipase work together?
en.sali_micelle: Bile salts surround fats, forming micelles.
en.lipasi_agisce: Here the pancreatic lipase can act and break down fats.
en.senza_bile: Without bile, lipase would not be able to digest fats properly.
en.movimenti_mescolamento: The small intestine moves in a special way to mix the chyme well.
en.movimenti_pendolari_desc: It doesn't push food forward continuously. It performs mixing movements, called pendular movements.
en.movimenti_allungano: Lengthen and shorten small sections of the intestine.
en.movimenti_mescolano: Mix the chyme with digestive juices.
en.movimenti_assorbimento: Promote contact with the villi for absorption.
en.titolo_funzione_crasso: The Function of the Large Intestine
en.crasso_ruolo_principale: The large intestine barely digests food anymore. Its main role is to absorb water and mineral salts from the material arriving from the small intestine.
en.crasso_feci_solide: This way, it transforms the liquid into more solid feces.
en.titolo_flora_batterica: Bacterial Flora: Friends Inside the Intestine
en.flora_desc: The large intestine contains billions of bacteria: this is the intestinal flora.
en.flora_vitamine: Produce certain vitamins (e.g., vitamin K and some B group vitamins).
en.flora_digerire_fibre: Help digest fiber and other non-digestible substances.
en.flora_difesa: Defend the intestine against bad bacteria.
en.flora_eccesso_problemi: Although useful, an excess of bacteria or the wrong bacteria can cause problems.
en.feci_non_solo_avanzi: Feces aren't just food leftovers. They are made up of:
en.feci_cellule_morte: Dead cells from the intestinal mucosa.
en.feci_spinta_retto: Feces are pushed towards the rectum with slow movements.
en.feci_stimolo_bagno: When the rectum fills up, there is an involuntary urge to go to the bathroom.
en.feci_espulsione: The expulsion occurs through the anus, controlled by the anal sphincter (a muscle that opens and closes).
en.bile_produzione: The liver continuously produces bile. About 1 liter per day.
en.bile_concentrazione: Most of it goes into the gallbladder, where it is concentrated.
en.bile_sostanze_concentrano: Water and other substances are concentrated.
en.bile_pigmenti: Bile pigments (e.g., bilirubin, from old red blood cells)
en.bile_enzimi_grassi: Small quantities of enzymes and fats
en.titolo_bile_rilascio: When does bile enter the intestine?
en.bile_rilascio_desc: Not always. Only during digestion. It exits the gallbladder and goes into the duodenum through the bile duct (choledochus).
en.bile_cck_stimolo: This release is stimulated by the hormone pancreozymin-cholecystokinin (CCK), produced by the duodenum when there is food.
en.titolo_bile_funzioni: What is the role of bile?
en.bile_funzione_lipasi: It helps lipase digest fats (by forming micelles).
en.bile_funzione_neutralizza: It neutralizes the acid from the chyme arriving from the stomach.
en.bile_funzione_assorbimento: It facilitates the absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
en.bile_funzione_protegge: It protects against excess bacteria thanks to its antiseptic action.
en.chilo_desc: After digestion, the contents of the small intestine become a dense, white liquid: it's called chyle.
en.fase_4_desc: Nutrients pass from the intestine into the blood and are carried throughout the body to provide energy and make organs work.
en.assorbimento_luogo: After digestion, the small intestine absorbs useful substances. This process mainly occurs in the intestinal villi.
en.villi_movimento_assorbimento: The villi move (lengthen and shorten) to allow substances to pass into the blood and lymphatic vessels.
en.assorbimento_sangue_titolo: The following substances go into the blood (through the villi capillaries):
en.circolo_vena_porta: These substances enter the mesenteric veins. They then form the portal vein, which carries everything directly to the liver.
en.circolo_generale: After the liver, the blood passes into the hepatic veins, then into the inferior vena cava, and returns to the general circulation.
en.linfatici_lattiferi_desc: These substances enter the lymphatic vessels of the villi (called lacteals).
en.linfatici_cisterna_pecquet: They go to the cisterna chyli (in the abdomen).
en.linfatici_dotto_toracico: They pass into the thoracic duct.
en.linfatici_vena_succlavia: The thoracic duct empties into the left subclavian vein.
en.linfatici_entrano_sangue: From there, they enter the bloodstream.
en.titolo_tenue_crasso: From the Small to the Large Intestine
en.passaggio_densita: As useful substances are absorbed, the intestinal content loses liquid and becomes denser.
en.spinta_crasso: Peristalsis pushes it towards the large intestine.
en.titolo_crasso_niente_digestione: In the Large Intestine: No Digestion, Lots of Transformation
en.crasso_no_enzimi: There are no enzymes in the large intestine. Therefore, no digestion occurs.
en.crasso_funzione_assorbimento_acqua: Absorption of water and mineral salts: the material becomes increasingly solid.
en.crasso_funzione_batteri: Action of bacteria: they ferment some fibers and produce gas and vitamins.
en.crasso_funzione_feci: Feces formation: indigestible residues, dead cells, mucus, and bacteria accumulate.
en.crasso_trasformazione_feci: Thanks to water absorption, the material becomes increasingly dense and transforms into feces.
en.crasso_movimento_lento: The large intestine moves slowly. Occasionally, it performs strong contractions called massive peristalsis.
en.crasso_movimento_spinta: These push the feces toward the rectum.
en.espulsione_stimolo: When the rectum fills up, the body feels the involuntary urge to go to the bathroom.
en.espulsione_sfintere: The expulsion is controlled by the anal sphincter: a muscle that can be opened and closed voluntarily.
en.espulsione_frequenza: Under normal conditions, feces are expelled once or twice a day, but everyone is different.

en.fegato_laboratorio: The liver doesn't only serve to produce bile. That's just one of its many functions. In reality, it is a major laboratory of the body.
en.fegato_peso_posizione: It weighs about 1500 grams. It is located in the upper right part of the abdomen.
en.fegato_riceve_sostanze: Substances absorbed from the intestine, via the portal vein.
en.fegato_riceve_rifiuti: Waste products produced by the body's cells.
en.fegato_funzione_amminoacidi: Produces essential amino acids: needed to build cell and blood proteins.
en.fegato_funzione_albumine: Synthesizes albumins: important proteins of blood plasma.
en.fegato_funzione_globuline: Synthesizes globulins: help blood clotting and the immune system.
en.fegato_funzione_glucosio: Transforms glucose into glycogen: stores it as an energy reserve.
en.fegato_funzione_metabolismo: Manages sugars and fats: regulates the metabolism of glucose and lipids.
en.fegato_funzione_innocue: Renders toxic substances harmless: such as alcohol, drugs, or body waste.
en.fegato_funzione_bile_comp: Produces cholesterol, bile acids, and bilirubin: main components of bile.
en.metabolismo_desc: Metabolism is the set of chemical reactions that allow the body to live, grow, and produce energy.
en.fase_anabolica: Anabolic phase (constructive): the body transforms food into energy or new matter. It is also called assimilation.
en.fase_catabolica_distruttiva: Catabolic phase (destructive): the body breaks down used substances. Waste exits through urine, sweat, and carbon dioxide.
en.bilancio_giovanile: In youth: the anabolic phase prevails → growth occurs.
en.bilancio_adulta: In adulthood: the two phases are in balance.
en.bilancio_vecchiaia: In old age: the catabolic phase prevails → mass and tissues are lost.
en.enzimi_desc: Metabolism depends on thousands of enzymes (ferments). There are about 25,000, and many more are yet to be discovered.
en.enzimi_condizione_acidita: The environment has the correct acidity.
en.enzimi_condizione_catalizzatori: Catalysts (like mineral salts or vitamins) are present.
en.reazioni_laboratorio: Many of these reactions cannot be reproduced in the laboratory. For example, the complete synthesis of very long proteins has only been partially achieved, and with the help of artificial systems.
en.omeostasi_desc: Normal metabolism maintains stable internal body conditions. This balance is called homeostasis.
en.metabolismo_basale_desc: It is the minimum amount of energy the body uses when it is at complete rest.
en.metabolismo_basale_serve_titolo: It is needed for essential functions such as:
en.metabolismo_basale_corrispondenza: Basal metabolism corresponds to cellular respiration.
en.misurazione_apparecchio: A special device that measures oxygen consumption is used.
en.misurazione_calcoli_titolo: Then, using calculations that take into account:
en.misurazione_fabbisogno_energetico: the daily energy requirement is estimated.
en.tiroide_desc: The thyroid gland influences the metabolism of all cells. If it produces too many hormones, metabolism speeds up. If it produces too little, it slows down.
